report:
## Conclusion

Yes — evidence indicates that widespread mask wearing can meaningfully reduce COVID-19 transmission at the population level, though the effect is moderate rather than absolute, and depends heavily on how many people actually wear masks and how well they fit.

The strongest real-world evidence comes from a large cluster-randomized trial in rural Bangladesh (342,183 adults), which found that community-level promotion of mask-wearing nearly tripled mask usage and reduced symptomatic, seroconfirmed SARS-CoV-2 infections by about 9–11% overall, with larger reductions (~30–35%) among older adults and with surgical masks specifically (science.org, https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abi9069). Modeling based on UK data similarly estimated that population-wide mask wearing reduced COVID-19 transmission by roughly 19%, contingent on high compliance (https://www.watoday.com.au/national/victoria/why-this-leading-modeller-thinks-you-should-put-your-mask-back-on-20220613-p5at7n.html). A JAMA review of accumulated evidence during the pandemic likewise concluded that community mask wearing helps control spread, especially given pre-symptomatic transmission (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2776536), and a 2023 JAMA Network Open analysis concluded that "robust available data support the use of face masks in community settings" (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2811136).

The widely publicized 2023 Cochrane review is often cited as contradicting this, but Cochrane's own editors clarified that its "no evidence" finding reflected weaknesses and heterogeneity in prior RCTs (mostly on influenza, with poor compliance) rather than proof that masks don't work — a point Cochrane explicitly addressed to correct misinterpretation (https://www.cochrane.org/news/statement-physical-interventions-interrupt-or-reduce-spread-respiratory-viruses-review).

Overall, when adopted broadly, masks appear to provide a real, though partial, protective effect against COVID-19 spread.
